title: Penance: Forgiveness after Baptism
lead: Can a Christian who sins seriously after baptism be forgiven, and how? The New Testament warns that those who fall away cannot easily be brought back (Hebrews 6:4-6; Hebrews 10:26) and also restores sinners in the church (2 Corinthians 2:5-11; James 5:19-20; 1 John 1:9). The Shepherd of Hermas (Rome, 100s) answered with 'one repentance' after baptism, and the question shaped the church's later practice of penance. Where the churches differ today, on a believer who falls and on confession to a priest, is set out on the cards at Hebrews 6 and Psalm 32.

sections.b: Hebrews says it is 'impossible to make them new again and bring them to repentance' those who have tasted the gift from heaven and then fallen away (Hebrews 6:4-6), and that for one who keeps sinning by choice 'there is no longer any sacrifice for sins left' (Hebrews 10:26). 1 John distinguishes sin 'not headed toward death' from sin that is (1 John 5:16). Paul tells the Corinthians to forgive and comfort a man who had been disciplined (2 Corinthians 2:5-11), and James to bring back one who wanders from the truth (James 5:19-20). Jesus tells Peter to forgive 'seventy-seven times' (Matthew 18:21-22). These texts were set against each other in the early church's arguments over whether, and how often, the baptized could be restored.
sections.refs: Hebrews 6:4-6; Hebrews 10:26; 1 John 5:16; 2 Corinthians 2:5-11; James 5:19-20; Matthew 18:21-22; 1 John 1:9

sections.h: Later practice: from one penance to repeated confession
sections.b: The Catholic Catechism describes how the practice changed. In the early centuries, Christians who had committed grave sins after baptism did a long public penance before they were reconciled, and in some regions admission to the order of penitents was 'only once in a lifetime'. From the seventh century Irish missionaries spread a private form of penance between penitent and priest, which 'envisioned the possibility of repetition' (Catechism 1447). The Catechism, after the Church Fathers, calls the sacrament of Penance 'the second plank [of salvation] after the shipwreck which is the loss of grace' (1446). This is the Catholic account. The other churches' views on confession and absolution, and on whether a believer can fall and be restored, are on the site's cards at Psalm 32 ('Must sins be confessed to a priest?') and Hebrews 6 ('Can someone who has truly believed fall away and be lost?').
